title: When AI Takes Notes: Court Allows Privacy Claims Against Otter.ai to Proceed

reading.body:
A transcription service used to record workplace meetings is alleged to have recorded and retained conversations without the knowledge or consent of all participants. The system was integrated with calendar and videoconferencing platforms in ways that reportedly enabled default recording without active opt-in from meeting attendees. A class-action lawsuit claims the service then used these recordings to train its AI system and did not adequately disclose this practice to participants.

The failure occurred at the point of deployment, where a system designed to transcribe meetings was set to record by default rather than requiring explicit consent from all parties before capturing audio. It would have taken a check at the moment of recording, before any audio was captured, to verify that all meeting participants had been informed and had agreed to be recorded and to have their conversations used for model training.

It is not established whether Otter's de-identification process was effective, whether users were actually deceived, or whether the company violated the laws cited in the complaint.

Enterprise note-taking apps face legal scrutiny as Otter hit with privacy suit

summary:
A federal lawsuit filed against Otter.ai, a Mountain View-based artificial intelligence transcription company, claims the company secretly records and shares private work conversations without permission. The suit alleges that Otter's transcription service, which works with Zoom, Google Meet, and Microsoft Teams, records meetings by default without asking all participants for consent and fails to inform them that recordings are used to train the AI system. Plaintiff Justin Brewer of San Jacinto, California contends his privacy was violated when he discovered confidential conversations were recorded without his knowledge. The lawsuit maintains that Otter violates state and federal privacy and wiretap laws and conducts this practice for financial gain.

The case comes as privacy concerns have mounted around Otter, which now has approximately 25 million users who have recorded over 1 billion meetings since the company's 2016 founding. Users have posted complaints on social media about the software automatically recording meetings when linked to workplace calendars. While Otter's privacy policy mentions that users can grant permission for AI training by checking a box, the lawsuit argues many users are still being deceived. The company claims it de-identifies audio data before using it for machine learning, but the suit questions whether this process effectively removes confidential information and guarantees anonymity.
